paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic model for motifs, recurring patterns in biopolymer sequences. Its central idea is to combine biological prior knowledge with dependencies between positions within a motif. This lets the model represent both which monomers are plausible at particular positions and how the distributions at different positions relate to one another.

The model uses a hierarchy of hidden variables. Each position has probabilities describing its monomer distribution, and those probabilities come from a mixture of Dirichlet distributions. A hidden Markov process determines which mixture component applies at each position. This connects the position-specific distributions through an underlying sequence of hidden states, rather than treating every position independently.

The authors fit the model to training motifs using variational expectation maximization within an empirical Bayesian framework. They also use variational inference to detect hidden motifs. They report higher detection sensitivity and better discrimination between genuine motifs and misleading recurring patterns than previous models that omit biological priors and positional dependence. These findings support combining both sources of structure when modeling motifs.
neurips-2002-a-hierarchical-bayesian-mar.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian motif model combines biological priors with positional dependencies to improve detection and distinguish genuine motifs from false recurring patterns.

paragraphs: The paper develops a recommendation method that uses a person's current sequence of navigation actions. It addresses settings where the item collection is large, observations are sparse, and behavior changes over time. Its maximum entropy formulation provides a framework for representing recommendations in the context of an unfolding browsing session.

The approach separates two challenges. First, it clusters items using patterns of user access, attempting to make recommendations that cross cluster boundaries unlikely in advance. It then recommends only within clusters, reducing the scope of the recommendation problem. Second, it represents the observations explicitly as a time series, allowing the model to account for their sequential organization rather than treating browsing activity as an unordered collection.

The authors evaluate the method using ResearchIndex, a repository containing more than 470,000 computer science documents. In offline tests that simulate recommending documents to users, their formulation outperforms several competing algorithms. The result supports this combination of clustering and temporal modeling for the evaluated recommendation setting; it is evidence from simulated recommendations rather than a reported live deployment.
neurips-2002-a-maximum-entropy-approach-.tldr: A maximum entropy recommender combines item clustering with navigation time series and outperforms several alternatives in offline document-recommendation tests.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately a population of neurons can represent and distinguish several stimuli presented at the same time. It introduces a framework that treats the features of all those stimuli together. The goal is to assess the information available about a combined presentation, rather than analyzing each stimulus as though it appeared alone.

The authors construct a compound space whose coordinates describe the features of every stimulus. They use Fisher information in that space to obtain minimal squared estimation errors. Even when neural responses simply add together and tuning follows a Gaussian shape, the resulting symmetries differ substantially from those for a single stimulus. Thus, simple response rules do not make the multiple-stimulus problem equivalent to separate single-stimulus problems.

The framework also permits a quantitative description of attentional effects. The authors state that it can be extended to incorporate neural nonlinearities, including nonclassical receptive fields. Its contribution is an estimation-based way to connect population responses with encoding accuracy and discrimination while explicitly retaining the structure introduced by simultaneous stimuli.
neurips-2002-an-estimation-theoretic-fra.tldr: A Fisher-information framework analyzes how neural populations encode multiple simultaneous stimuli and how their joint structure changes estimation accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies the structure of optimal solutions for related objectives in rate distortion theory, deterministic annealing, information distortion, and the information bottleneck method. Its focus is on bifurcations: points where branches of solutions emerge or change their arrangement. Understanding this structure means examining how optima relate to one another, rather than only locating an individual solution.

The authors introduce a methodology for determining that branching structure for a class of similar cost functions drawn from these approaches. Treating the objectives together provides a shared way to study their optima. The scope is a related class of objectives, so the contribution concerns the common mathematical structure identified within that class.

The paper also introduces a numerical algorithm that uses explicit expressions for the branching solutions to find optima at a bifurcation point. This links the structural analysis to computation: information about the branches becomes part of the procedure for finding a solution. The stated contribution is both a method of analysis and an algorithm built around the structure that analysis reveals.
neurips-2002-annealing-and-the-rate-dist.tldr: The paper analyzes branching optima in related information-theoretic objectives and introduces an algorithm that uses those branches to find optima at bifurcation points.

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian framework for building speech-recognition models and using them to recognize speech. Called variational Bayesian estimation and clustering, or VBEC, it constructs shared-state triphone hidden Markov models. The framework brings model estimation, clustering, and predictive classification into a common Bayesian approach.

A central concern is choosing an appropriate model structure when training data are limited. The authors contrast their approach with conventional maximum-likelihood methods using criteria such as BIC or MDL. VBEC does not rely on an asymptotic assumption, meaning that its model-selection rationale does not require the large-data approximation used by those conventional criteria. The authors therefore describe its selection procedure as valid in principle even with insufficient data.

In isolated-word recognition experiments, VBEC shows an advantage over conventional methods, especially with small training sets. These results connect the model-selection argument to observed recognition performance. The claim is that the framework can find suitable structures with strong recognition performance, with the reported experimental advantage particularly relevant to situations where examples are scarce.
neurips-2002-application-of-variational-.tldr: A variational Bayesian framework selects speech-model structures without an asymptotic assumption and improves isolated-word recognition, especially with limited data.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how syntactic knowledge can be learned directly from text corpora without supervision. It starts from the distributional principle: morphemes appearing in identical contexts can be regarded as belonging to a common category in some sense. This makes patterns of usage a source of evidence about linguistic structure.

The authors extend that principle recursively, allowing the same idea to participate in building increasingly structured representations. They also use mutual information to estimate category coherence, providing a statistical basis for assessing the groupings. Together, these components produce distributed representations of syntactic knowledge, with structure learned from the corpus rather than supplied through category labels.

The resulting model exhibits promising behavior on tasks commonly associated with grammar-based representations, including systematicity. This suggests that recursively organized distributional information can support some behavior usually attributed to an explicit grammatical organization. The reported finding is promising performance on such tasks, rather than a claim that the model captures every aspect of syntax or fully replaces grammar-based accounts.
neurips-2002-automatic-acquisition-and-e.tldr: Recursive distributional learning and mutual information produce structured syntactic representations with promising behavior on tasks such as systematicity.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to make unlabeled examples useful to a kernel classifier. Its guiding assumption is that two points belonging to the same cluster are more likely to share a label. This gives the organization of the data a role in classification even when the labels themselves are available for only part of the data.

The method introduces that information by changing the eigenspectrum of the kernel matrix. A kernel matrix represents similarities among examples, while its eigenspectrum describes aspects of the structure of those similarities. Modifying it provides a route for cluster information to influence the representation used by the classifier. The unlabeled data therefore contribute through the kernel rather than through additional observed labels.

The authors report experiments assessing the validity of this approach. The central contribution is the connection between a cluster-based assumption and a concrete change to the kernel representation. The assumption remains probabilistic: points in a common cluster are considered more likely to share a label, without requiring every cluster to contain only one class.
neurips-2002-cluster-kernels-for-semi-su.tldr: Cluster kernels incorporate unlabeled data by modifying a kernel matrix's eigenspectrum under the assumption that cluster membership is informative about labels.

paragraphs: The paper examines when reinforcement-learning updates converge while using linear function approximation. Transition sampling can affect convergence, yet practical applications may need to reuse transitions collected from different sources. The authors study a specific version of this problem: repeated synchronous updates performed on a fixed collection of transitions.

Their main theorem gives sufficient conditions for convergence of combinations of learning algorithms and linear approximators. This makes compatibility between the update rule and the representation a subject of explicit analysis. Sufficient conditions establish when convergence is supported by the theorem; they do not imply that every combination outside those conditions must fail.

For one particular pairing, residual gradient learning with grid-based linear interpolation, the authors establish the existence of a universal constant learning rate that yields convergence independently of the particular transition data. This is a stronger data-independence result for that specified combination within the studied setting. The paper therefore offers both a general compatibility framework and a concrete example where convergence does not depend on which fixed transitions were collected.
neurips-2002-convergent-combinations-of-.tldr: The paper gives sufficient convergence conditions for reinforcement learning with linear approximation and a data-independent constant-rate guarantee for one specific pairing.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a sparse Gaussian-process framework designed to reduce both prediction cost and the resources needed for training. It uses forward selection, choosing a compact set through information-theoretic criteria previously suggested for active learning. The goal is to retain useful predictive information while working under tight time and memory constraints.

With n training points and a sparse representation of size d, where d is much smaller than n, predictions require O(d) work instead of O(n). The method's scaling is at most O(n d²). These properties address two distinct needs: making the trained predictor economical to evaluate and keeping construction of that predictor manageable.

In large real-world classification experiments, the method can match support vector machine prediction performance while training significantly faster. The authors also emphasize that their approximation produces predictive probability estimates, supports Bayesian model selection, and has a less complex implementation than the SVM. The reported result is a combination of competitive classification, potentially substantial training savings, and probabilistic outputs, rather than a universal speed or accuracy advantage.
neurips-2002-fast-sparse-gaussian-proces.tldr: Information-based forward selection yields sparse Gaussian-process predictors that can match SVM accuracy while training faster and retaining probabilistic predictions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses uncertainty about whether different observations refer to the same underlying object. Its application is citation matching: deciding which bibliographic references describe the same publication. This is difficult when identifiers are missing or imperfect and author names or titles appear in corrupted forms.

The authors build a relational generative probability model that includes author and title corruption together with a probabilistic grammar for citations. They represent uncertainty directly over possible mappings from terms in the representation to real objects. Inference uses Markov chain Monte Carlo, supplemented by proposal methods designed to work efficiently when many objects are present.

On several citation datasets, the method outperforms the citation-matching algorithms used for comparison. Its relational structure also supports recovering object characteristics, such as author names, by combining evidence across citations of multiple papers. The contribution therefore extends beyond deciding whether a pair of references matches: it provides a joint probabilistic account in which uncertain identities and shared object information can be inferred together.
neurips-2002-identity-uncertainty-and-ci.tldr: A relational probabilistic model jointly resolves citation identities and object attributes, outperforming comparison methods on several citation datasets.

paragraphs: The paper learns document representations from paired English texts and their French translations without category labels. The translation pairs provide two expressions of shared content. The aim is to extract features useful for retrieval, categorization, or clustering, including tasks that connect documents across languages.

Each language is represented using kernel functions, specifically bag-of-words inner products. Kernel canonical correlation analysis then finds directions in the two representation spaces that correlate maximally. The semantic interpretation rests on an explicit assumption: the two representations are independent apart from their semantic content. Under that assumption, recurring correlations between English and French word patterns should reflect shared meaning.

The authors first show that the learned cross-language correlations are significantly greater than random, supporting the presence of statistical structure that should reflect semantic information. They then evaluate the representation in both single-language and cross-language retrieval. On the same data, performance is consistently and significantly better than latent semantic indexing. These results support translation-based correlation as a useful source of document features in the evaluated retrieval tasks.
neurips-2002-inferring-a-semantic-repres.tldr: Kernel correlation analysis learns document features from English–French translation pairs and improves both single-language and cross-language retrieval over LSI on the evaluated data.

paragraphs: The paper considers low-rank approximation methods that represent data through a lower-dimensional space. Examples include principal components analysis and latent semantic analysis. Such techniques generally operate without labels or categories, which makes them useful when those annotations are unavailable but leaves open how to use other knowledge that may already exist.

The author focuses on prior information supplied by context. The proposed approach provides a principled way to incorporate that information into a projection. The key idea is that constructing a compact representation need not depend only on the observed data considered without context; relevant knowledge can also inform how the approximation is formed.

The paper demonstrates the approach through PCA-based approximations of several datasets. These applications show how the general idea can be used within an established projection method. The contribution is a way to connect contextual knowledge with low-dimensional representation learning, illustrated through those approximations. It addresses the practical middle ground in which a problem lacks explicit labels but still comes with useful information about the setting.
neurips-2002-informed-projections-2c5036.tldr: Informed projections incorporate contextual prior knowledge into low-dimensional approximations, with demonstrations using PCA on several datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning visual properties by finding features that change slowly as inputs vary. Earlier slow feature analysis projects inputs into a nonlinear space and extracts slowly changing directions there. This can reveal higher-order invariances, but the dimensionality of that nonlinear representation had restricted the approach to simple theoretical simulations.

The authors use a different, closely related objective for slowly varying features and apply the kernel trick. This allows the nonlinear computation to be expressed through kernel evaluations, avoiding the stated dimensionality obstacle. The change matters because it makes the slow-feature approach applicable to learning from natural images in the setting studied.

Using the new method, the authors show that translation invariance and disparity coding can be learned simultaneously as properties of complex cells. These modeled cells receive inputs from simple cells that are also learned from the images. The finding supports a learning account in which both properties emerge together from natural-image input through a hierarchy of learned visual responses.
neurips-2002-kernel-based-extraction-of-.tldr: A kernel-based slow-feature method learns translation invariance and disparity coding together from natural images while avoiding the stated dimensionality obstacle.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a relationship between one class of objects and another, potentially different class. The objects may be vectors, images, strings, trees, or graphs. This formulation makes the output itself part of the representation problem, rather than assuming that every prediction must already have a simple numerical form.

The approach uses kernel functions to measure similarities in both the input and output spaces. These kernels embed the respective objects into vector spaces, providing a mathematical setting in which their dependency can be learned. The central move is therefore to represent relationships among possible outputs as well as relationships among inputs.

The authors experimentally validate the approach on string-to-string mapping, pattern recognition, and reconstruction from partial images. These tasks illustrate its use across different kinds of input-output relationships. The contribution is a common kernel-based formulation for learning between object domains: suitable similarity measures provide a route from structured objects to vector-space learning, even when the two sides of the mapping contain different kinds of objects.
neurips-2002-kernel-dependency-estimatio.tldr: Kernel dependency estimation uses similarities on both inputs and outputs to learn mappings between general objects such as strings and images.

paragraphs: The paper treats the choice of a kernel as something to learn from data. Its objective is to construct an accurate kernel from simpler base kernels that are individually less accurate. This places the learning effort partly in the similarity representation used by a classifier, rather than only in the classifier operating on that representation.

The authors adapt boosting to work with kernel operators. They also design an efficient weak learner for simple kernels using generalized eigenvector decomposition. These components provide both a process for building the overall kernel and a procedure for finding the simpler kernels used within that process.

The approach is demonstrated on synthetic data and the USPS dataset. On USPS, a Perceptron using the learned kernels performs systematically better than one using a fixed radial basis function kernel. This result supports learning the kernel for the evaluated classification problem. The reported comparison concerns the Perceptron and those kernel choices, while the broader methodological contribution is adapting boosting to kernel construction.
neurips-2002-kernel-design-using-boostin.tldr: Boosting combines simple learned kernels into a stronger kernel, improving Perceptron performance over a fixed RBF kernel on USPS.

paragraphs: The paper asks why some images are perceived as two transparent layers and how a visual system might choose a particular decomposition. An image can be written as the sum of two component images in infinitely many ways, including the trivial choice of the original image plus nothing. The percept therefore requires a principle for preferring some explanations over others.

The authors suggest that transparency can be understood as a rational percept for a system adapted to natural-scene statistics. They construct a probabilistic image model using qualitative statistics of derivative-filter and corner-detector responses. The model seeks the most probable decomposition of a new image, with optimization carried out using loopy belief propagation.

On synthetic images, the model produces decompositions that the authors describe as perceptually correct. They also discuss application to real images. The demonstrated result supports the proposed statistical explanation in the synthetic setting: natural-image regularities can help select a perceptually appropriate layered interpretation from the many decompositions mathematically available.
neurips-2002-learning-to-perceive-transp.tldr: A probabilistic model based on natural-scene statistics produces perceptually appropriate transparency decompositions on synthetic images.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a simplified model inspired by neurons in the fly brain can estimate self-motion from optic flow. These neurons respond to visual motion patterns characteristic of the animal's own movement. The study asks how far a linear combination of local flow vectors can go toward recovering that movement.

The authors develop a theory for constructing such an estimator while incorporating prior knowledge. That knowledge includes the distribution of distances in the environment, sensor noise, and the statistics of self-motion. The estimator therefore combines observed flow with information about the surroundings and sensing conditions when determining how the flow vectors should contribute.

The method is tested physically using a gantry equipped with an omnidirectional vision sensor. The experiments produce accurate and robust estimates of rotation rates, while translation estimates are less reliable. This distinction is central to the finding: the simplified linear neural model works well for rotation in the reported tests, but its success does not extend equally to every component of self-motion.
neurips-2002-linear-combinations-of-opti.tldr: A fly-inspired linear optic-flow estimator gives accurate, robust rotation estimates in physical tests, while translation estimates are less reliable.

paragraphs: The paper develops a model for separating speech from a single audio channel. It addresses a weakness of earlier auditory-scene-analysis systems: difficulty handling speech at high frequencies. Motivated by psychoacoustic evidence, the model uses different processing strategies for resolved and unresolved harmonics instead of applying one grouping mechanism throughout the signal.

For resolved harmonics, it forms segments using continuity over time and correlations across channels, then groups those segments by periodicity. For unresolved harmonics, segmentation also uses amplitude modulation, and grouping follows modulation repetition rates estimated through sinusoidal modeling. A pitch contour obtained under psychoacoustic constraints underlies the separation process.

The model is systematically evaluated and substantially outperforms previous systems, with particularly strong improvement in the high-frequency range. The finding supports using distinct signal cues for the two harmonic regimes. Its contribution is not just the presence of a pitch estimate, but the organization of segmentation and grouping around the different information available in low- and high-frequency speech.
neurips-2002-monaural-speech-separation-.tldr: A single-channel speech-separation model uses different cues for resolved and unresolved harmonics, substantially improving performance, especially at high frequencies.

paragraphs: The paper derives multiplicative update rules for the nonnegative quadratic programming problem arising in support vector machines. The updates optimize the conventional SVM objective and have a simple closed form. The authors prove monotonic convergence to the solution defining the maximum-margin hyperplane.

The method avoids heuristic choices such as setting a learning rate or selecting which variables to update at each step. All quadratic-programming variables can be adjusted in parallel, with a guarantee of improvement at each iteration. This makes the update mechanism straightforward while connecting its repeated application to the original optimization objective.

The authors also analyze behavior near convergence. Coefficients associated with non-support vectors decay geometrically toward zero, at rates determined by their margins. This explains how examples that do not support the final boundary lose influence during optimization. In practice, the updates are reported to reach good classifiers very rapidly. The paper thus combines a monotonic convergence result, a more detailed account of coefficient decay, and an empirical observation about useful classifiers emerging quickly.
neurips-2002-multiplicative-updates-for-.tldr: Closed-form multiplicative SVM updates permit parallel optimization without learning-rate heuristics and provably converge monotonically to the maximum-margin solution.

paragraphs: The paper introduces rational kernels, a general family of similarity functions based on weighted transducers or rational relations. They apply to variable-length sequences and, more generally, weighted automata. This gives sequence-analysis problems in areas such as speech recognition and computational biology a shared way to construct kernels.

The authors show how to compute these kernels efficiently through weighted-transducer composition and a general single-source shortest-distance algorithm. They also identify several broad families of symmetric positive-definite rational kernels. These results connect expressive sequence comparisons with reusable computational procedures and kernel properties suitable for learning methods.

Combined with support vector machines, the kernels yield substantial classification-accuracy improvements in spoken-dialog classification. The authors emphasize that complex kernels become easier to design and implement within this framework. They further show that the string kernels considered in computational-biology applications are special cases of rational kernels. The contribution therefore includes both an applied classification result and a unifying representation for previously considered sequence kernels.
neurips-2002-rational-kernels-bbe4067e45.tldr: Rational kernels unify sequence similarities through weighted transducers, support efficient computation, and improve spoken-dialog classification when paired with SVMs.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the connection structure of an articulated body from observations of its moving parts. Such structures are often represented as trees in human-body tracking. Here, the rigid motion of each constituent segment is assumed to be known; the task is to learn how those segments are connected.

The authors search for a maximum-likelihood tree-shaped factorization of the joint probability distribution of segment motions. In plain terms, they choose a tree-structured statistical description that best accounts for the observed motions under their model. The topology of the resulting graphical model corresponds to the topology of the articulated body.

The method is demonstrated on both synthetic data and real motion-capture data. Its contribution is a learning-based route from observed segment motions to an articulated connection structure. The known-motion assumption is essential to understanding the scope: the method addresses recovery of the tree topology once segment motions are available, rather than presenting the entire process of extracting and tracking those segments from raw observations.
neurips-2002-recovering-articulated-mode.tldr: Given known rigid-segment motions, the method learns an articulated body's topology through a maximum-likelihood tree factorization.

paragraphs: The paper reconsiders what replay might contribute to memory consolidation. A standard account holds that episodes are stored temporarily in the hippocampus and transferred to the neocortex through replay. The authors note experimental challenges to this transfer account, particularly for human memory, that motivate reconsidering its interpretation.

A key distinction is between evidence that replay occurs and an explanation of its purpose. The abstract points to independent neurophysiological evidence for replay even as the transfer hypothesis faces challenges. This leaves a computational question: what useful role could replay serve if its function is not adequately explained by moving episodic memories between brain systems?

The authors suggest and demonstrate two computational roles associated with neocortical indices. Their contribution is to offer additional functional accounts of replay in a setting where theoretical alternatives to transfer were scarce. The significance lies in separating a supported neural phenomenon from one particular explanation of it, and in investigating computational roles that preserve a place for replay while the standard consolidation account is being reevaluated.
neurips-2002-replay-repair-and-consolida.tldr: The paper proposes and demonstrates two computational roles for replay associated with neocortical indices as alternatives to a transfer-centered account.

paragraphs: The paper adapts boosting to unsupervised learning by turning density estimation into a sequence of classification problems. It builds a random field model one feature at a time. Each new feature is trained to distinguish observed data from an equally sized set of negative examples generated by the current model.

Every round has three stages. The method first samples negative examples from the model's Boltzmann distribution. It then trains a feature to improve discrimination between those samples and the data. Finally, it learns a coefficient controlling the feature's importance relative to those already included. Negative examples need to be generated only once for each new feature.

This creates its own classification signal without requiring externally supplied class labels: the distinction is between actual observations and the model's current samples. The authors demonstrate the approach on binary digits and continuous synthetic data. These demonstrations support using sequential discriminative feature learning to construct an unsupervised density model, extending the boosting idea beyond its more established classification and regression settings.
neurips-2002-self-supervised-boosting-18.tldr: Self-supervised boosting builds a density model by repeatedly learning features that distinguish observed data from samples generated by the current model.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a replanning method for nondeterministic domains, where actions can have more than one possible outcome. Its aim is to make repeated planning efficient. The authors describe the method as an incremental heuristic minimax search algorithm and qualify the novelty claim as the first such algorithm to their knowledge.

The method brings incremental search together with minimax planning. Incremental replanning concerns updating a plan as the planning problem changes, while the minimax formulation addresses alternative outcomes in the nondeterministic setting. The contribution is the combination of these ideas in an algorithm intended to make that replanning process efficient.

The authors apply it to the dynamic discretization of continuous domains, where a discrete representation is adjusted during the solution process. This produces an efficient implementation of the parti-game reinforcement-learning algorithm for control in high-dimensional domains. The connection matters because replanning and representation changes are treated together: a search method designed for changing planning problems becomes a computational component of the parti-game approach.
neurips-2002-speeding-up-the-parti-game-.tldr: An incremental heuristic minimax replanning algorithm enables an efficient parti-game implementation for control in high-dimensional continuous domains.

paragraphs: The paper examines the relationship between loopy belief propagation and the Bethe free energy. These provide two perspectives on the same inference problem: an iterative algorithm and an optimization objective. The authors investigate what the stability of an algorithmic fixed point implies about its position in the objective's landscape.

They transform constrained Bethe free-energy minimization into an unconstrained saddle-point problem. Both converging double-loop algorithms and ordinary loopy belief propagation can then be interpreted as attempts to solve that problem. This shared formulation allows stability analysis to connect the behavior of the iterations with the character of the corresponding stationary solutions.

The main conclusion is directional: stable fixed points of loopy belief propagation must be local minima of the Bethe free energy. The reverse implication does not always hold, because a minimum can correspond to an unstable fixed point. The authors illustrate this with an example. Thus, identifying a local minimum alone does not establish that ordinary belief-propagation iterations will remain stable around it.
neurips-2002-stable-fixed-points-of-loop.tldr: Stable loopy-belief-propagation fixed points are local Bethe free-energy minima, but some such minima can be unstable fixed points.
